reconcile.connective: Gill argues both animals were literally brought and dressed with garments, so Matthew's plural "them" need not mean Jesus rode both at once.

discrepancy.connective: Bart Ehrman presses the sharper reading: Matthew literalized Zechariah's Hebrew parallelism into two real animals, with Jesus straddling both as he rode into the city.

skeptic.name: Bart D. Ehrman
skeptic.work: Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible
skeptic.attribution: Bart D. Ehrman, Jesus, Interrupted: Revealing the Hidden Contradictions in the Bible (HarperOne, 2009), p. 50

excerpts.excerpt_text: And brought the ass and the colt,.... To Jesus, as Mark and Luke add, and who only make mention of the colt: both were undoubtedly brought; the colt being unloosed and taken away, the ass, its dam, followed after: … and they sat him thereon, or "on them": meaning either on the ass and colt, that is, on one of them, or both successively, or on the clothes they put upon them.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Gill names the exact tension (Mark and Luke mention only the colt) and glosses Matthew's 'sat...on them' as meaning one animal, both successively, or the garments — a direct harmonization of the two-animal wording with the single-colt Synoptic/Johannine accounts.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley prints the parallel Matt 21:2-3 / Mark 11:2-3 / Luke 19:30-31 accounts of sending for the ass and colt and dismisses the alleged one-or-two-animals discrepancy as ordinary variation among independent witnesses — the same tension the riding scene in Matt 21:5-7 raises.

link.note: Live apologetic treatment arguing both animals were present but Jesus rode only the colt, the mother accompanying as a calming presence.
